deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page continues the Pallas work of the previous folio. There Gauss fitted the elliptic elements to the oppositions of 1805–1809 and obtained corrections x=+14.57" to the perihelion (giving 120°57'28.70") and y=−3.04" to φ (giving φ=14°9'39.50"). The adopted mean tropical daily motion is n=770.93546". Times t are counted in days from 1803 Jan 0. This page does two things: (A) it predicts the 1811 opposition of Pallas, and (B) it tabulates Jupiter's perturbations of the Pallas elements at the oppositions.

A1. Mean longitudes, epoch Jan 0 of 1802–1811. The list is 143°13'22.36", 221°23'13.81", 299°45'56.19", and so on. Successive differences are 78°09'51.44" for 365 days and 78°22'42.38" for 366 days (after the leap years 1804 and 1808).
- 78°09'51.44" = 281391.44", and 281391.44/365 = 770.935", which is n.
- 281391.44 + 770.935 = 282162.38" = 78°22'42.38".
So the table is just L0 + n·t, with Jan 0 1803 = 221°23'13.81" taken from the previous page.

A2. Meridian correction. The heading reads 'Göttg. +1.61"'. At the right, 3.233 min of time /1440 = 0.002245 d, noted as 'Seeberg − Göttingen = 0.0022 d'. The 1811 epoch longitude is changed from 127°7'47.23" to 127°7'48.84" (+1.61").

A3. Date and precession. The date is 1811 Feb 22, 16h, so t = 2975.7 (log 3.47358). The daily precession is 0.13717"/d (log 9.13725); this equals the tropical minus sidereal daily motion on the previous page, 770.93546 − 770.79829. Precession for 2975.7 d is therefore 408.16".
- Perihelion: π = 120°57'28.70" + 6'48.16" = 121°4'16.86".
- Node: Ω = 172°28'2.00" + 6'48.16" = 172°34'50.16".

A4. Mean anomaly. The mean longitude is 127°7'48.84" + 11°29'33.34" (motion in 53.667 d). Gauss writes 138°37'22.38". Then M = L − π = 17°33'5.52".

A5. Kepler's equation, E = M + e" sin E.
- log e" = log sin φ + log 206265 = 4.7029649.
- With log sin E = 9.5925343, e" sin E = 5°29'6.91", so E = 23°2'12.44".

A6. Radius vector.
- log e cos E = 9.3885398 + 9.9639076, so e cos E = 0.2251372.
- log(1 − e cos E) = 9.8892247.
- With log a = 0.4420439: log r = 0.3312686, r ≈ 2.144.

A7. True anomaly, using Theoria Motus art. 8: sin ½(v−E) = sqrt(a/r) · sin ½φ · sin E.
- ½log(r/a) = 9.9446123½.
- log sin E − ½log(r/a) = 9.6479219½.
- Adding log sin ½φ = 9.0908345 gives 8.7387565, so ½(v−E) = 3°8'28" and v − E = 6°16'56.70".
- v = 29°19'9.14".

A8. Argument of latitude.
- ω = π − Ω = 308°29'26.70" (mod 360).
- u = v + ω = 337°48'35.84".

A9. Reduction to the ecliptic, with i = 34°37'12".
- tan(l−Ω) = cos i · tan u: 9.6105428 + 9.9153672 = 9.5259100, so l − Ω = 341°26'41.07".
- Heliocentric longitude l = 154°1'31.23".
- sin b = sin i · sin u: 9.5771239 + 9.7544485 = 9.3315724, so b ≈ −12°23'.
- log cos b = log cos u − log cos(l−Ω) = 9.9665811 − 9.9768162, giving 0.0102351 in absolute value. This is the curtate-distance reduction.
- Two further logs, 9.7033096 and 9.6899077, are not identified.

A10. Sun's place, in signs-degrees-minutes-seconds.
- Mean longitude: 9s9°44'13.3" + 1s22°14'20.5" + 8'36.6" (+0.4") gives 11s2°7'11.8".
- Solar perigee: 9s9°40'24" + 9" = 9s9°40'33".
- Mean anomaly: 1s22°26.65' (= 52°26'39").
- Equation of centre: +1°31'56.6".
- Two small terms are added: 7.1" (unidentified, perhaps nutation) and 25.4".
- The 25.4" comes from the argument table M A B C D E F N (Delambre/Zach solar tables). The perturbation sums are 25.49" (21 Feb) and 25.03" (1 Mar); interpolation to Feb 22.67 gives 25.4".
- Result: Earth's heliocentric longitude (Sun + 180°) is 153°39'40.9".

A11. Opposition. Pallas leads Earth by 21'50" at Feb 22.67. Dividing by the relative motion places the opposition at 'Feb 23, 4h, in 154°11''.

B. Perturbation table: 'Störungen der Elemente der Pallas durch den Jupiter, die Elemente von 1803, 156t als Normalelemente betrachtet'. The osculating reference epoch is t = 156 d of 1803.
- Rows are the opposition dates t = 181.0, 608.2, 1064.4, 1585.6, 2034.9, 2457.7, 2976.1. They correspond to 1803 Jun 30, 1804 Aug 31, 1805 Nov 29, 1807 May 4, 1808 Jul 26, 1809 Sep 22, 1811 Feb 23.
- Columns give the perturbations δi, δΩ, δω, δφ, δε (epoch) and δ(50μ) (change of mean motion per 50-day quadrature interval). The final column 'Integr.' is ∫δμ dt, the perturbation of mean longitude from the changed mean motion.
- An earlier pair of columns, δ50μ and ∫δ50μ dt, all positive (+0.839 … +3434.79), is struck out. It is replaced by a negative δ50μ column (−0.585 … −93.633) and a negative integral (0 … −2403.93). This is evidently a sign or computation correction.
- A rough trapezoid in 50-day units with only the opposition values reproduces the integral column to within about 10%. This is consistent with a finer quadrature at 50-day steps.

These values feed the perturbed least-squares fit of Pallas's elements.
errors: 127°7'48.84" + 11°29'33.34" = 138°37'22.18", but 138°37'22.38" is written and then used. This is either a 0.2" slip or a misreading of one of the digits; it propagates into M = 17°33'5.52".
The +1.61" Göttingen correction does not equal n × 0.002245 d (= 1.73"); it corresponds to about 0.00209 d. It may rest on a different longitude difference or have another origin (unsure).
The last row is labelled VIII although it is the seventh opposition listed (VII). This is possibly a numbering slip, or VII was reserved for something else.
The first δ50μ and ∫δ50μ dt columns (all positive) were wrong and are struck out by Gauss himself; the replacement column has the opposite sign and smaller integrated values.

results.what: Mean-longitude ephemeris of Pallas by uniform tropical mean motion 770.935"/day, with precession 0.13717"/day applied to node and perihelion
results.modern_name: Mean longitude / precession reduction of osculating elements

results.what: Solution of Kepler's equation and true anomaly via sin½(v−E)=sqrt(a/r) sin½φ sinE
results.modern_name: Kepler equation solution; Gauss's half-angle formula (Theoria Motus art. 8)

results.what: Prediction of the 1811 opposition of Pallas (Feb 23, 4h, longitude 154°11') from corrected elements and solar tables
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Pallas ephemerides published in Monatliche Correspondenz)

results.what: Table of Jupiter's perturbations of Pallas's elements (i, Ω, ω, φ, ε, mean motion and its integral) at the oppositions 1803–1811, relative to osculating elements of 1803 day 156
results.modern_name: Special perturbations by variation of elements with mechanical quadrature
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange/Laplace (variation of constants); applied to Pallas by Gauss 1810–1812

deep.surprise_reason: This is working material for Gauss's well-documented Pallas computations (opposition ephemerides and Jupiter perturbations, c. 1810–1812). The methods are those of Theoria Motus and standard variation of elements; only the specific numbers are unpublished detail.

log of eccentricity in arcseconds equals 4.7029649
Kepler's equation E = M + e sinE holds for M=17°33'5.52", E=23°2'12.44"
tan(l−Ω) = cos i tan u gives l−Ω = 341°26'41.07"
log sin|b| = log sin i + log sin u = 9.3315724

transcription_corrections: '22,16t febr' should read '22 16h febr' (Feb 22, 16 hours), consistent with t = 2975.7.
'0,22513725' is e·cosE = 0.2251372 (a trailing 5 is probably a stray digit).
'9,9446123½' and '9,6479219½' are logarithms with a final half-unit (…1235, …2195), not fractions to be applied.
'[?] 36,6' in the solar column is probably '8 36,6' (8'36.6").
'(134019)' refers to the log 0.0134019 from the previous page; '102351' is log cos b = 0.0102351 (in absolute value).
